edits.definition: A State is a politically organised community of people permanently occupying a definite territory, served by an organised government to which the bulk of the inhabitants render habitual obedience, and exercising sovereignty — supreme authority over its internal affairs, free from external control. The four accepted elements are therefore population, territory, government and sovereignty; all four must exist together. India, for example, is a State in this sense, while a tribe without settled government or a province within a federation is not. In Legal Studies the term 'State' is always used in this technical sense, never as shorthand for a regional unit.

Administrative law is the body of legal principles that governs the creation, powers, procedures and control of administrative authorities — ministries, departments, regulators and tribunals of the executive wing. It ensures that delegated rule-making and discretionary decisions remain within the statute that grants them, that affected persons receive a fair hearing (the rules of natural justice), that decisions are reasonable and not arbitrary, and that remedies exist when authorities exceed their powers, chiefly through writs and judicial review by the higher courts. It is judge-made and statute-made law about the administration, not the law the administration makes for citizens' private dealings.

Administrative law is the branch of public law that regulates the organisation, powers and procedures of administrative authorities — ministers, civil servants, regulators and tribunals — and the control exercised over them. It requires delegated legislation to stay within its parent Act, discretionary action to follow the rules of natural justice (no one may judge their own cause; both sides must be heard), and it exposes illegal, irrational or procedurally unfair decisions to judicial review. Its twin purposes are to equip the administration with workable powers and to protect the citizen against their abuse.

Administrative law governs the processes and procedures by which administrative authorities — government departments, regulators and tribunals — take decisions affecting the rights and liabilities of citizens. Its core principles are legality (power must trace back to a statute), procedural fairness through the rules of natural justice (the hearing rule and the rule against bias), reasonableness of discretionary decisions, and accountability through remedies: appeal, writ jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court, and judicial review. The subject thus explains both how delegated legislation and adjudication are carried out lawfully and how the citizen challenges them when they are not.

Answering framework questions from the jurisprudence chapter demand a mapped, mark-aware method. Very short answers (1-2 marks) reward precise definitions — the meaning of law, natural justice, or one school of law stated in two or three lines. Short answers (3-4 marks) require a concept explained with one example or distinction, such as positive law versus natural law. Long answers (5-6 marks) expect a stated position, developed arguments citing more than one school of thought or the Speluncean Explorers hypothetical, and a reasoned conclusion. Structuring every answer — define, develop, conclude — converts textbook knowledge into board-ready responses.

The classification of laws by process distinguishes substantive law from procedural (adjective) law. Substantive law creates, defines and regulates rights, duties and liabilities — the Indian Contract Act stating when an agreement binds, or the Indian Penal Code stating what is punishable, are substantive. Procedural law prescribes the machinery for enforcing those rights and liabilities: the modes of bringing a suit, the pleading and evidence rules, appeals and execution, as laid down in the Civil Procedure Code and the Criminal Procedure Code. The substantive rule answers 'what is the law?', the procedural rule answers 'how is it enforced?' — both are needed for any remedy.

The classification of laws is the systematic arrangement of legal rules into categories that make study and application orderly. By subject matter, law divides into criminal law (offences against the State and society, punishable with fine, imprisonment and the like) and civil law (rights and duties between individuals). By function, into substantive law, which defines rights and duties, and procedural law, which supplies the machinery of enforcement. By reach, into international law governing relations between States, and municipal (national) law, which further divides into public law concerning the State-citizen relationship and private law governing person-to-person relations. Classification identifies the correct rule, remedy and forum.

Sources of law are the origins and foundations from which legal rules derive their validity, authority and binding force. The three principal sources in the modern Indian legal system are custom — long-established practice accepted as law; judicial precedent — the principles declared by superior courts while deciding cases, binding on lower courts under the doctrine of stare decisis; and legislation — the statutes enacted by the legislature, which today is the most important and prolific source. Jurists also distinguish primary sources from persuasive ones such as professional opinion and foreign judgments, and identify justice, equity and good conscience as subsidiary sources applied where none of the main sources covers a dispute.

Sources of law are the origins from which legal rules receive their validity and binding character. Custom is the oldest source: a practice followed voluntarily and continuously by a community, which the courts recognise as law when it is ancient, reasonable, continuous and not against statute. Judicial precedent is the source consisting of the legal principles laid down by higher courts in decided cases, which bind subordinate courts and guide later benches. Legislation — Acts made by Parliament and State Legislatures — is the supreme and most productive modern source, capable of overriding custom and modifying precedent, and it now supplies most of the working rules of Indian law.

Sources of law are the foundations from which the rules of the legal system draw their authority. In India three sources matter most. Custom — practice observed steadily and openly by a community — supplied much of Hindu and Mohammedan law and is still recognised where it is ancient, certain, reasonable and consistent with statute. Judicial precedent — the law declared by the Supreme Court and High Courts in the cases they decide — binds all lower courts and fills gaps where statutes are silent. Legislation — Acts of Parliament and State Legislatures, plus delegated rules made under them — is the dominant modern source, because the legislature can make, change or repeal law deliberately and in advance.

Law reform is the systematic examination and revision of existing law — by amendment, consolidation, codification or repeal — and, where necessary, the enactment of new law, so that the legal system keeps pace with changing social values, economic conditions, technology and constitutional mandates. In India the formal machinery includes the Law Commission of India, which undertakes studies and submits reports recommending change, the parliamentary committee system, which scrutinises bills, and judicial decisions that press legislatures to act. Reform examples range from criminal-law amendments and the replacement of old codes to information-technology and consumer-protection statutes created for needs earlier law never contemplated.

Law reform is the continuing process by which a legal system reviews, amends, replaces or repeals its laws so that they remain just, workable and responsive to the society they govern. It is triggered by changed social values, new technology, constitutional requirements and the practical failures of existing provisions. The institutional agents are the Law Commission of India and other expert committees, the parliamentary legislative process, and public consultation; judicial decisions may expose the need for reform but the remaking of law belongs to the legislature. Illustrations include the modernisation of criminal procedure, the evolution of consumer protection law, and statutes created for the digital economy.

Law reform is the structured process of reviewing existing laws and changing them — by amendment, repeal or fresh enactment — so that they keep step with changing social, economic and technological realities while respecting constitutional rights. Reform may be corrective (removing defects courts have exposed), consolidating (gathering scattered provisions into one Act) or innovating (creating law for new situations such as cyberspace). The regular agents are the Law Commission of India, expert and parliamentary committees, and the legislature itself; boardsexam questions usually expect the agency, the trigger and one worked example of a successful reform to be named together.

Cyber law in India is the body of legal rules governing activity in cyberspace, anchored in the Information Technology Act, 2000 and its amendments, together with allied provisions of the Indian Penal Code and sectoral data rules. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, regulates e-commerce and electronic filing, defines and punishes offences such as unauthorised access, identity theft, data theft, cyber-terrorism and publication of obscene material, and prescribes duties and liabilities for intermediaries and certifying authorities. Its purpose is to make the digital environment trustworthy: transactions enforceable, data protected, and wrongdoers answerable in court.

Cyber law is the branch of law that deals with legal questions arising from computers, computer networks and the internet. Its subject matter includes cybercrimes (hacking, identity theft, stalking, data theft and their punishment), the validity of electronic contracts and signatures, the liability of intermediaries such as websites and service providers, the protection of personal data, and intellectual property in digital form. In India the foundational statute is the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with amendments and penal provisions, which together give electronic records the same legal effect as paper records and attach consequences to unlawful acts committed online.

Child rights are the fundamental entitlements and protections that every human being below eighteen years of age possesses simply because of being a child. Following the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, 1989) and Indian constitutional and statutory law, they are grouped as the rights to survival (life, health, nutrition), development (education, play, culture), protection (from abuse, exploitation, trafficking and hazardous work) and participation (expression and being heard in matters affecting the child). The State, parents and society share the duty to realise them; instruments such as the Juvenile Justice Act and the Right to Education Act convert them into enforceable Indian law.

Judicial review is the power of the constitutional courts — the Supreme Court and the High Courts — to examine the actions of the legislature and the executive, and to declare them void where they violate the Constitution. Its principal objects are legislation, executive orders and administrative action infringing fundamental rights (Articles 32 and 226 provide the remedy), and constitutional amendments damaging the basic structure of the Constitution. Established in India through the decisions in A.K. Gopilan, elaborated after Kesavananda Bharati, judicial review is regarded as part of the basic structure itself: it keeps every organ of government within the limits the Constitution sets.

A contract is an agreement enforceable by law, as defined in Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872: every promise and every set of promises forming the consideration for each other which, on satisfying the statutory essentials, the law will enforce. The essentials are offer and acceptance creating a lawful agreement, free consent of the parties, capacity to contract (majority, sound mind, not disqualified), lawful consideration, a lawful object, and intention to create legal relations, with the agreement not expressly declared void. When these are present the obligations created become legally binding; if any essential fails, the agreement remains a bare promise or becomes void or voidable as the case may be.

A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement becomes a contract when it unites the essential elements: an offer by one party and its unqualified acceptance by the other, free consent not obtained by coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, capacity of the parties to contract, lawful consideration moving between them, a lawful object, and an intention to create legal obligations, with nothing in the agreement expressly declared void. Satisfy these and the promises become binding obligations whose breach is actionable; miss one and there is no contract, only an agreement.

The processes and procedures of the law of torts are the machinery by which a claim for a civil wrong is brought, fought and enforced in India. A claim begins with the choice of the proper forum — the civil court of competent jurisdiction determined by the place of the wrong and the value of the claim — followed by pleadings (the plaint stating facts and the cause of action, and the written statement), framing of issues, production and appreciation of evidence, and interim remedies such as injunctions and attachment before judgment. The judgment is then enforced through execution; appeals and review provide correction. Procedural codes govern these steps because torts have no single procedural statute of their own.

Practice in criminal-law questions is built on applying the three pillars of Indian criminal law — the Indian Penal Code defining offences, the Criminal Procedure Code governing investigation and trial, and the Indian Evidence Act governing proof — to concrete fact situations. Model answers show the discipline required: distinguishing intention from motive when deciding culpability, identifying the exact stage of crime (preparation, attempt, commission) and its consequence for liability, matching an accused's act to the ingredients of the offence before naming it, and stating the evidentiary rule that decides what the court may consider. Scenario-based answers earn marks by citing the principle, applying it to the facts, and concluding with the result.

Human rights are the entitlements that belong to every person because of their humanity alone — held equally by all, regardless of nationality, race, sex, religion, language or status, and inalienable in the sense that they cannot be taken away except in circumstances defined by law. They span civil and political rights (life, liberty, equality before the law, free expression), and economic, social and cultural rights (work, education, health, an adequate standard of living). Their modern charter is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the covenants that followed it; in India they are protected through the Constitution, the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 and the courts.

International law is the body of rules and principles that governs the relations of States with one another and with other subjects of international life, such as international organisations. Its acknowledged sources under Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice are treaties (express agreements that bind their parties), international custom (general practice accepted as law), and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations, with judicial decisions and scholarly writing as subsidiary aids. Lacking a world legislature and central police, its enforcement depends on consent, reciprocity, diplomatic pressure and collective measures — yet it structures diplomacy, trade, sea passage, armed conflict and human rights across borders.
